title: Optimisations
text:
A few optimisations were introduced to improve the speed of the code, allowing us to perform operations on larger system sizes in much shorter timeframes.
Firstly, the Python library Numba was implemented to some functions, which drastically increased the speed at which the program executed. Numba is a just-in-time compiler, which compiles certain functions directly machine code, making them faster at runtime. Python is somewhat an interpreted language, which means that a line is “translated” into machine code as it is run. However, Python is actually compiled into bytecode before running, which is a simplified version similar to assembly; this is done to increase the interpretation speed. Regardless, compiling direct to machine code reduces the workload of the interpreter, and hence the function runs much faster.
Numba doesn’t work particularly well with certain libraries and functions within Python, however it does work with Numpy, which is the primary maths module used here. Numpy is already fast at certain tasks (most parts that require fast computation are written in C or C++), and so this in combination with Numba should produce excellent results.
In fact, upon running functions with the Numbra wrapper enabled (mcmove as an example, the function to run the Monte Carlo evolution), evolving the system runs approximately 10 times faster - a massive speed increase.
A few other quality-of-life optimisations were made. The code was refactored into separate Python files, and then imported into the main Jupyiter notebook for ease of access. New modules listed below were added to improve usability.

tqdm provides loading bars for iteration in Python. This provides valuable information about roughly how long a loop will take to run, and hence time is not wasted waiting for a “random” amount of time.
reload automatically refreshes imported files, which is critical here when using a Jupyiter notebook.

As well as this, the code was rewritten to include a more consistent and readable variable name structure, to improve its understandability and readability.

title: Introduction
text:
The Ising model (or Lenz-Ising model) is a theoretical model often used to describe Magnetism, which is often best utilised numerically (in fact, it is currently impossible to solve generally). It helps to explain the effect of ferromagnetism, wherby magnetic moments align despite the removal of an applied magnetic field.
It also provides great insight into phase transitions, whereby a material changes state (such as water boiling in a kettle to become steam).
The Ising model has had many other uses, such as uses statistically modelling neuron activity [1] and hence a natural extension has been found with neural networks, as well as to model the motion of atoms in gases.
[1]: Elad Schneidman; Michael J. Berry; Ronen Segev; William Bialek (2006), “Weak pairwise correlations imply strongly correlated network states in a neural population”, Nature, 440 (7087): 1007–1012, arXiv:q-bio/0512013, Bibcode:2006Natur.440.1007S, doi:10.1038/nature04701, PMC 1785327, PMID 16625187

title: Theory
text:
Describing the model
Consider some lattice of atoms. In this lab, the main focus is on a square lattice in two dimensions.
It is assumed that each atom has a magnetic moment, or spin, of either up or down. More detailed models allow the atoms to be in “superpositions” of these two choices, but here it is assumed that they are one or the other. This spin is denoted
\[\sigma_i = \pm 1\]
where spin up is \(+1\) and spin down is \(-1\).



A 2D square lattice, with atomic spins labelled.


The energy of the system can be represented using the Hamiltonian, usually defined as the sum of the potential and kinetic energy. Here, the energy depends on external fields, denoted \(B\), and also the nearest neighbour atomic spins. The latter is a result of it being energetically favourable for a spin to align with its neighbours. Thus, the Hamiltonian for the system can be defined as
\[
    H=-\sum_{i,j}J \sigma_i \sigma_j - \sum_i B \sigma_i
\]
The constant \(J\) represents the exchange energy, which is essentially the energy required to “flip” a spin. The minus sign in front of the first sum is to ensure that it is favourable for nearby spins to be aligned.
